title: Framing Effect
description: Making decisions based entirely on how information is presented to us, rather than the raw facts themselves.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: It's not what you say, it's how you say it. We react violently differently to the exact same information depending on whether it is presented as a 'gain' or a 'loss'.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Loss aversion. The brain hates losing things far more than it likes gaining things. When a choice is framed as a 'gain', we feel safe. When the exact same choice is framed as a 'loss', we panic and take immediate risks to avoid it.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: Business: Selling ground beef as '95% fat-free' instead of '5% fat'.
Sales: Calling a price increase a 'Late fee' versus calling a discount an 'Early bird special'.
Politics: Framing a tax explicitly as 'Government funding' versus a 'Tax burden'.
Health: A doctor explaining an operation has a '90% survival rate' instead of a '10% mortality rate'.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Scenario A (Loss Frame): 'If you don't buy this home insulation, you will lose $500 a year in energy costs.'
Scenario B (Gain Frame): 'If you buy this home insulation, you will save $500 a year.'
Result: Scenario A reliably sells vastly more insulation because humans are terrified of losing money.

sections.title: Pattern Recognition
content: Focusing heavily on what you will lose if you don't act immediately.
Changing the names of negative things to sound positive (e.g., 'pre-owned' instead of 'used').
Using extreme percentages instead of raw, absolute numbers.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Presenting health choices or financial data with balanced frames (clearly showing both the risks and the benefits) so people can make fully informed decisions.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Deliberately spinning identical data to obscure massive, fatal risks. Using a terrifying 'loss frame' to panic vulnerable people into buying useless insurance.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Emotional buzzwords that rapidly alter your perception without presenting any actual new hard data.
Hearing identical statistics presented with dramatically different connotations depending on which news channel you watch.
A heavy reliance on percentages without ever showing the absolute numbers.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Reframe the sentence in your own head to the exact opposite before deciding anything.
Translate specific ratios and percentages into hard, absolute numbers.
Ask: 'What is the base rate? Does a 100% increased risk just mean it went from 1 to 2?'

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Assuming their decision was perfectly logical, when they were actually just emotionally reacting to the framing.
Letting words like 'loss', 'penalty', or 'danger' shut down their critical thinking.

sections.title: Case Study
sections.content: Researchers gave participants a hypothetical scenario: A deadly disease is about to strike a town of 600 people. You must choose a vaccine program. When framed as a gain ('Program A will save 200 people'), people safely chose A. When framed as a loss ('Program A means 400 people will die'), people overwhelmingly violently rejected A and chose a risky gamble instead. The math was completely identical. The words completely dictated the final choice.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: 1. It's not the facts; it's the frame.
2. Fear of loss drives action much harder than the promise of gain.
3. Always flip the frame in your head before committing.
4. Look at the raw numbers, ignore the adjectives.
